failures.title: Volvo D4204T Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: EGR Cooler & Intake Carbon Buildup - 2012-2019 production
items.whatHappens: Excessive carbon deposits build up in the intake system. The intake valve can leak, causing intake air temperature to rise - which can melt and deform the engine intake manifold. In extreme cases, this can cause the engine to stop or even lead to an engine bay fire. Volvo issued a UK recall in November 2019 covering vehicles with the D4204T8 engine code manufactured between 2012 and 2019.
items.repairVsReplace: EGR cooler replacement and intake manifold cleaning typically resolves the issue if caught early. If the manifold has deformed or melted, replacement is mandatory. Many owners report that EGR replacement alone does not always cure oil consumption issues, suggesting piston ring or turbo seal wear in higher-mileage units. Read our full EGR failure guide

items.title: Oil Consumption - D4204T5 and D4204T16 variants
items.whatHappens: Some D4204T engines - particularly the D4204T5 (181hp) and D4204T16 (150hp) - exhibit excessive oil consumption, with reports of 8.4 litres per 10,000 km (approx. 1 litre per 1,200 miles). This often appears after EGR-related software updates or replacements, suggesting a link between EGR strategy changes and oil consumption patterns. Compression tests often remain good (96-100%), pointing to turbo seals, valve stem seals or piston ring gumming rather than bottom-end wear.
items.repairVsReplace: Turbocharger inspection and replacement of valve stem seals can reduce consumption, but in advanced cases a full rebuild or replacement is the only definitive fix.

items.title: Timing Belt - interference engine, critical interval
items.whatHappens: The D4204T uses a timing belt, not a chain. As an interference engine, a failed belt - or a failed tensioner or water pump driven by the belt - causes pistons to strike valves, destroying the cylinder head and often the bottom end. The belt interval varies: D4204T5 (181hp) and D4204T14 (190hp) require replacement at 150,000 km (approx. 93,000 miles) or 10 years.
items.repairVsReplace: Belt failure is catastrophic - full engine replacement is almost always required. Preventative belt replacement at the correct interval is essential; many specialists recommend replacing the water pump and auxiliary belt simultaneously. Read our full timing belt failure guide

failures.goodYearsLine: Post-2016 D4204T units (particularly D4204T14 and D4204T23 variants) incorporated revised EGR cooling and updated software, with fewer reports of the extreme carbon buildup that triggered the 2019 recall. The D5 (235hp) twin-turbo variant is generally considered more robust than earlier single-turbo D4 tunes.

variants.title: D4204T Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: The D4204T is a VEA (Volvo Engine Architecture) family engine - one physical design with multiple sub-codes distinguished by power output, turbo configuration and ECU calibration. Getting the right sub-code matters: a D4204T4 (150hp) and D4204T14 (190hp) share the same block but differ in turbo, injectors and software - they are not straight swaps. - Fitted to: V40, S60, V60, XC60, XC70, XC90 (AWD variants) - Key technical difference: Single turbo, lower boost calibration, 150hp / 350Nm. The entry-level VEA diesel in AWD form. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family EGR and oil consumption patterns; no distinct failures reported. - Interchange note: Not a direct swap with D4204T14; turbo, injectors and ECU calibration differ. - Fitted to: V40, S60, V60, XC60, S80, V70 - Key technical difference: Single turbo, higher boost, 181hp / 400Nm - the most common D4 tune in the UK. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Most frequently reported oil consumption issues (8.4L/10,000km) - see Section 5. - Interchange note: Shares block with D4204T14 but requires different injectors and ECU; not a straight swap. - Fitted to: V60, XC60, XC90 AWD - Key technical difference: Single turbo, 190hp / 420Nm - higher torque than the FWD D4 tune. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares family pattern; no distinct failures. - Interchange note: AWD-specific oil pan and sump differ from FWD variants. - Fitted to: V40, S60, V60, XC60 - Key technical difference: Lower-power D3 tune, 150hp - entry-level diesel. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares family EGR issues. - Interchange note: Early D4204T7 units (2010-2012) have different DPF and AdBlue configurations from later variants. - Fitted to: V40, V40CC, V60, S60 - Key technical difference: 181hp D4 tune - subject to the November 2019 UK recall for intake manifold melting / fire risk. - Sub-code-specific failure note: The recall specifically covers D4204T8 (engine code 74). If your car has this code and the recall work hasn't been done, check with a Volvo dealer immediately. - Interchange note: Post-recall units have revised EGR and intake components; ensure any replacement engine has had the recall work performed. - Fitted to: V40, S60, V60 - Key technical difference: 150hp D3 tune, lower output than D4. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Some oil consumption reports - see Section 5. - Interchange note: Shares most components with D4204T4; check turbo part numbers. - Fitted to: V40, S60, V60 - Key technical difference: Lowest-output VEA diesel, 120hp - often in entry-level V40 D2. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Lower-stressed; fewer failure reports than higher-output D4 variants. - Interchange note: Different turbo and injectors; not interchangeable with D4 sub-codes. - Fitted to: XC40 - Key technical difference: 190hp D4 AWD tune for the XC40 platform. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares family pattern. - Interchange note: XC40-specific engine mount and accessory drive layout differs from 60/90-series. - Fitted to: V40, V60, S60, XC60, XC90, S90, V90 - Key technical difference: 190hp / 400Nm - the most powerful single-turbo D4 tune, introduced from 2015. Latest VEA diesel before the switch to mild-hybrid. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Improved EGR design; fewer carbon buildup reports than earlier D4204T5/T8. Timing belt interval: 150,000 km (93,000 miles). - Interchange note: Later D4204T14 units (2017+) have different software and injector part numbers; check compatibility carefully. - Fitted to: V40, S60, V60, XC60, XC90 - Key technical difference: Updated D3 tune, 150hp - post-2014 calibration. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Oil consumption reported on higher-mileage examples. - Interchange note: Shares most hardware with D4204T4; ECU calibration differs. - Fitted to: V90, XC90 - Key technical difference: Late D4 calibration, 190hp - primarily SPA-platform vehicles. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Fewer reports than earlier variants; improved EGR. - Interchange note: SPA-platform engine mounts and ancillaries differ from P3-platform (V60/XC60 pre-2018). - Fitted to: XC90, V90, XC60 - Key technical difference: Twin-turbo (sequential) - 235hp / 480Nm. The flagship VEA diesel. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Twin-turbo complexity adds potential turbo actuator and boost control issues - but generally considered more robust than single-turbo D4 units.

relatives.description: D5204T (2.4L D5): The five - cylinder 2.4-litre D5 that preceded the VEA family - a completely different engine architecture, smoother and more characterful, but heavier, thirstier and with its own set of issues (intercooler splitting, swirl flap failure). The D4204T was Volvo's move to a modular four-cylinder platform for emissions compliance.

D4204T14 (updated D4): The later 190hp revision of the same VEA diesel, introduced from 2015 with improved EGR cooling and a revised timing belt interval. If you're replacing a D4204T5 or D4204T8, the D4204T14 is the preferred donor - it benefits from the engineering learnings from the earlier failures.

B4204T (2.0 T5 petrol): The petrol counterpart in the VEA family - a turbocharged 2.0-litre four-cylinder that shares the same block architecture but is fundamentally different in fuelling, compression and ancillaries. The D4204T is the diesel variant; if your car is petrol, you're on the wrong page.

relatives.code: The VEA diesel is a Volvo-only engine and was never shared with other manufacturers. Unlike the older 2.0D (PSA/Ford DW10) used in early S40/V50/C30/C70, the D4204T is pure Volvo design

variants.closing: The D4204T sub-code is printed on a label on the timing belt cover and in the V5C registration document. You can also use Volvo's VIN decoder - the 6th-8th characters of the VIN identify the engine code. Enter your registration above and we'll confirm your exact sub-code before any quotes are sent.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement D4204T - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used D4204T can make sense for older, lower-value V40, S40 or V50 hosts where the car's value doesn't justify a £2,500+ recon unit. **Crucially:** only buy a used unit with documented EGR recall work (if D4204T8) and timing belt history - a used engine without these is a gamble that rarely pays off. D4204T5 and D4204T8 units with oil consumption issues should be avoided unless the price reflects the risk. Used engines service

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper D4204T recon addresses the EGR cooler, intake manifold carbon cleaning, timing belt and tensioner, water pump, and injector seals - exactly the failures that take out these engines in service. This is the right call for any car worth over £4,000 where you plan to keep it for 2+ years. Most recon units come with a 12-month warranty and known service history. Reconditioned engines service

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full D4204T rebuild is rarely cost-effective compared to a reconditioned exchange unit - the labour to strip, assess and rebuild a VEA diesel with new pistons, rings, bearings and a cylinder head overhaul typically exceeds £3,500 before parts. Only consider a rebuild for a low-mileage, high-spec car (e.g. XC90 D5 Inscription) where the chassis is worth preserving and you have a specialist who knows the VEA platform intimately. Rebuilt engines service

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All replacement engines through our network are supplied with 12-month warranty and can be fitted by Volvo specialists nationwide. Supply & fit service
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The D4204T sits across a wide value range - from £2,000 V40 D2s to £25,000 XC90 D5s. For a V40 or S40/V50 valued under £3,000, a reconditioned engine at £2,500-£3,500 may represent 80-100% of the car's value - evaluate scrap value before committing. For XC60, XC90 and V90 owners, the car's retained value comfortably absorbs a recon engine cost. Be honest about the car's condition, mileage and MOT history before deciding.

items.question: What is the common failure on the D4204T engine?
items.answer: The most widespread issue is EGR cooler and intake manifold carbon buildup, which affected the D4204T8 variant enough to trigger a UK recall in November 2019. Carbon deposits can cause the intake manifold to melt and deform - in extreme cases, this can lead to engine stoppage or fire. Secondary issues include excessive oil consumption (particularly on D4204T5 and D4204T16), and the timing belt is an interference design - failure is catastrophic. EGR recall applies to D4204T8 (engine code 74). Oil consumption can reach 8.4L per 10,000km on affected units. Timing belt interval: 93,000 miles or 10 years.

items.question: Which Volvo models have the D4204T engine?
items.answer: The D4204T was fitted across almost the entire Volvo range from 2010 to 2018 - from the V40 hatchback through to the XC90 SUV. The highest-volume UK applications are the V40 (2012-2019), S60 (2010-2018), V60 (2010-2018), and XC60 (2010-2017). It also appears in S80, V70, XC70, S90, V90, C30, C70, S40 and V50. Badge names: D2 (120hp), D3 (150hp), D4 (181-190hp), D5 (235hp). Check your V5C or timing belt cover label for the exact sub-code.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned D4204T engine?
items.answer: It depends on your car's value. For a V40 or S40 valued under £3,000, a used unit with documented history (£900-£1,800) may be the only financially sensible option - but only buy if the EGR recall work (if applicable) and timing belt are done. For XC60, XC90, S90/V90 owners where the car is worth £8,000+, a reconditioned unit (£2,500-£4,500) with a 12-month warranty and all known issues addressed is almost always the better long-term investment. Used: lower upfront cost, higher risk of inheriting the same failures. Reconditioned: all common failure points addressed, 12-24 month warranty. Always insist on documented EGR history and belt change.

items.question: What's the difference between D4204T5, D4204T8 and D4204T14?
items.answer: These are all VEA 2.0-litre diesel sub-codes with different power outputs and revisions. D4204T5 is the 181hp D4 tune (2010-2015) - the most common UK variant and most frequently reported for oil consumption. D4204T8 is the 181hp D4 (2012-2019) that was subject to the EGR/intake manifold fire recall. D4204T14 is the later 190hp D4 (2015+) with improved EGR cooling and a longer timing belt interval - considered the most reliable of the three. D4204T5: 181hp, early single-turbo, oil consumption risk. D4204T8: 181hp, recall variant - check if recall work done. D4204T14: 190hp, revised EGR, best choice for replacement.

items.question: How long does a D4204T engine last?
items.answer: With proper maintenance, 150,000-200,000 miles is achievable before major work is needed. The key factors are: (1) strict adherence to the 93,000-mile / 10-year timing belt interval - failure is catastrophic; (2) EGR system maintenance - early D4204T5/T8 units need carbon cleaning around 80,000 miles; (3) oil changes at 12,000 miles or annually with the correct 0W-20 VCC RBS0-2AE spec. Many D4204T units in XC90s and V60s exceed 200,000 miles with the EGR issues addressed proactively. Timing belt is the single most important service item. EGR-related failures typically emerge between 60,000-100,000 miles. Regular motorway driving (DPF regeneration) extends lifespan.
